scope: Self-proclaimed DPR/LPR-controlled areas in Donetsk and Luhansk regions from 2014 through the eve of Russia's 2022 full-scale invasion. The artifact separates media-infrastructure capture, content/narrative production, audience exposure, measured effects, coercion and confounders.
terminology_note: DPR/LPR labels are used as historical names for the self-proclaimed entities; their claimed sovereignty was not internationally recognized. The file does not treat propaganda as the sole cause of political attitudes or conflict outcomes.
claim_ceiling: Armed groups and DPR/LPR authorities rapidly seized or controlled broadcast infrastructure and forced replacement of Ukrainian/local programming with Russian or DPR/LPR-aligned programming in 2014.
The information environment was subsequently institutionalized through ministries of information, accreditation rules, media legislation, repurposed outlets and newly created websites/newspapers.
Recurring narratives demonized Ukraine/the Kyiv government, emphasized war costs and alleged atrocities, and used fear/anger-heavy emotional framing.
Russian television exposure had measurable persuasive effects in Ukraine in 2014, but effects were heterogeneous and could backfire among strongly pro-Western audiences.
The long-term Donbas propaganda project was not omnipotent or ideologically coherent; pre-existing preferences, coercion, war experiences, local grievances and identity are major confounders.

timeline.finding: OSCE reported that armed/unidentified uniformed actors seized the Donetsk regional television and radio company and a regional transmission centre and replaced some local broadcasts with Rossiya 24.

OHCHR reported severe curtailment of media freedom: Ukrainian TV channels were switched off and replaced by DPR media and Russian TV. Armed groups pressured TV Channel Union in Donetsk; Vokar Holding was forced under threat to stop retransmitting Inter, Ukraina, 1+1, ICTV, STB, Novyi Kanal, Channel 5, 112 Ukraine and TVI in Severodonetsk, with Russian channels broadcast instead; similar incidents occurred across Luhansk region.

OHCHR documented abduction/threats against editors of Donbas and Vecherniy Donetsk to force more positive DPR coverage; a Donetsk cable/Internet provider also terminated several Ukrainian channels at DPR representatives' demand.

OSCE reported a DPR decree requiring media outlets to register with a self-proclaimed information ministry; the OSCE representative condemned pressure forcing outlets to report in favor of illegal armed groups.
OSCE reported that staff of Luganskoye Kabelnoe Televideniye were forced to leave their building by armed separatists and transmission was replaced by Russian Channel 5.

Cambridge research describes a two-stage process: destruction of the pre-existing media structure through coercion/exit/repurposing, followed by reconstruction via new channels, repurposed outlets, ministries, accreditation and media legislation. Around forty DPR/LPR news websites were created between 2014 and 2018.

documented_disinformation_and_hate_examp.example: OHCHR documented DPR-linked hate speech and a 'Holy War' statement including language about exterminating America on an official media outlet.

LifeNews used an older photograph of a wounded child from Aleppo while presenting it as a child wounded at Donetsk airport; OHCHR also documented reuse of an unrelated 2010 Crimea child-death photo and unrelated videos presented as current Ukrainian atrocities.

Russian Channel One aired the uncorroborated 'crucified boy' story alleging a three-year-old was publicly crucified by Ukrainian forces in Sloviansk. Contemporary fact-checking found no evidence or corroborating witnesses; Channel One later acknowledged it lacked evidence to confirm the account.

narrative_families.name: DELEGITIMIZE_KYIV
narrative_families.evidence: Cambridge research identifies sustained efforts to delegitimize Ukraine and portray it as an illegitimate or failed polity.

narrative_families.name: DEMONIZE_OUTGROUP
narrative_families.evidence: Academic content analysis found the outgroup—Ukraine/the Kyiv regime—was richly and repeatedly demonized; online outlets emphasized shaming the enemy, alleged war crimes and deliberate obstruction of peace.

narrative_families.name: GENOCIDE_AND_EXISTENTIAL_THREAT
narrative_families.evidence: The genocide/Nazi frame persisted from 2014 into later DPR/LPR and Russian messaging and was repeatedly catalogued by EUvsDisinfo and academic research.

narrative_families.name: BUSINESS_AS_USUAL_NORMALIZATION
narrative_families.evidence: DPR/LPR print and online media mixed conflict narratives with ordinary local reporting, helping normalize the entities as everyday political communities.

narrative_families.name: RUSSIA_KINSHIP_AND_MEMORY
narrative_families.evidence: Print-media research found collective-memory and kinship themes, although the positive ingroup identity remained less coherent than the negative construction of Ukraine.

audience_and_effect_evidence.finding: An Internews/InMind survey found that in Donetsk region 62% reported watching Russian TV and 57% trusted Russian TV; 77% watched Ukrainian news but only 24% trusted it. Television was the dominant news source nationally.
audience_and_effect_evidence.interpretation: Shows high exposure and trust asymmetry, not causal proof by itself.

audience_and_effect_evidence.finding: Peisakhin and Rozenas used plausibly exogenous variation in Russian analog-TV availability and found Russian TV substantially increased support for pro-Russian candidates/parties in Ukraine's 2014 elections; evidence favored persuasion rather than differential mobilization.
audience_and_effect_evidence.interpretation: Strong causal evidence that biased television can affect political behavior under some conditions.

audience_and_effect_evidence.finding: The same study found effects were heterogeneous: strongest among audiences with pro-Russian priors and weaker or counter-persuasive among strongly pro-Western audiences.
audience_and_effect_evidence.interpretation: Critical falsifier against an omnipotent-propaganda model.

audience_and_effect_evidence.finding: Cambridge's 2024 synthesis concludes years of Russian/proxy influence were at least somewhat successful in fostering anti-Ukrainian sentiment in Russia and to an extent in DPR/LPR areas, but broadly backfired in Ukraine, strengthening Ukrainian identity especially among Russian-speaking Ukrainians.
audience_and_effect_evidence.interpretation: Propaganda effectiveness is conditional, nonlinear and audience-dependent.

confounds_and_falsifiers: Donbas had significant pre-existing pro-Russian, regional-autonomy and separatist preferences before media capture; attitudes cannot be attributed solely to propaganda.
2014 KIIS survey evidence indicates strong but not unanimous separatist sentiment in Donbas; support for joining Russia was far below unanimity.
War casualties, coercion, displacement, local grievances, party identity, ethnicity and direct military events independently shape attitudes.
Ukraine also restricted Russian television during the conflict; OSCE criticized blanket channel bans and emphasized pluralism.
DPR/LPR ideological identity-building was fragmented and often ad hoc rather than a perfectly coherent master narrative.
Russian propaganda could polarize or backfire among audiences predisposed against it.

comparison_with_crimea_2014.crimea: FAST_BLITZ_CAPTURE: transmitter control and source substitution largely completed before the 16 March referendum.
comparison_with_crimea_2014.donbas: LONG_DURATION_CAPTURE: seizure/pressure in spring-summer 2014 followed by institutional media reconstruction, censorship law and years of narrative production.
comparison_with_crimea_2014.important_difference: Donbas offers a multi-year laboratory of normalization, identity construction and conflict-memory narratives rather than Crimea's compressed takeover window.

transfer_to_tspu_external_warning.historical_analogy: Physical transmitter/cable capture can be functionally analogous to digital distribution control when a network layer selectively removes external sources and leaves aligned substitutes reachable.
transfer_to_tspu_external_warning.warning: The Donbas case proves that distribution control and narrative operations can be integrated over years; it does not prove exported TSPU will be remotely activated by Russia in sovereign third countries.
transfer_to_tspu_external_warning.measurement_requirement: Any future warning must independently measure reachability, route/fingerprint, substitute availability, narrative timing and audience response.

next_gates: Build a day-level 2014 Donetsk/Luhansk channel-by-channel replacement timeline.
Code DPR/LPR/Russian narrative frequency from April 2014 through 2022 using replicable corpora.
Separate Russian federal media, DPR/LPR official media, local coerced media and organic local voices.
Pair audience surveys with source availability and trust data rather than inferring belief from content volume.
Use causal-media studies and backfire findings as permanent constraints in the US-risk model.
